recognise: Two black pines stand directly opposite each other on the Main Walk: one with slender downward-sloping limbs, the other with huge upward-spreading branches and an open crown.
verify_notes: Garden page: Main Walk grouping of Black/Austrian Pine subspecies, 'large, mature trees date from the earliest plantings in the 1840s'; garden established 1846. Most extreme contrast is the pair ssp nigra (Austria, downward-sloping unbranched limbs, short stiff needles) opposite ssp salzmannii (Spain, immense upward-spreading branches, open canopy of long needles); nearby ssp pallasiana (Crimean) and ssp laricio (Corsican). Placed deliberately by John Stevens Henslow, Darwin's mentor, to show variation within a species; positioned in the high-profile spot where symmetry would be expected. cam.ac.uk news 8 May 2023: the black pine was lit by pedal-power in the Coronation concert on 7 May 2023, 'one of the first Garden plantings' (alive evidence, 2023; garden page current). Age derived from garden's 1840s planting statement for the group, not a per-tree date; no girth or height given anywhere. Both sources are the owner (garden and university): one owner, flagged. Pin is the garden's centroid (Wikipedia 52.19361, 0.12722), not the tree; garden is 16 ha, tree position within it not fixed from a source. One collectible point: the opposed pair, one place to stand. Garden's separate black-pine trail page exists (learning/trails/speciation/blackpine) but not fetched.
story:
Darwin's teacher planted these pines so that they would look wrong. John Stevens Henslow, the botanist who mentored Charles Darwin at Cambridge, set out the Botanic Garden's Main Walk with black pines facing each other in pairs, exactly where a visitor expects symmetry, and then chose trees that refuse to match.

The starkest pair stands directly opposite one another. On one side is the Austrian form, with slender, unbranched limbs sloping downward and short, stiff needles. On the other is the Spanish form, its immense branches spreading upward into an open crown of long needles. Same species, different countries, and the difference is the lesson. Crimean and Corsican black pines stand nearby to make the point twice more.

The garden says its large black pines date from the earliest plantings of the 1840s, soon after it was established in 1846, which puts the pair at roughly 180 years. It gives no planting date for either tree on its own, and no girth or height has been published.

They are still part of the garden's life rather than its archive. On 7 May 2023, during the Coronation concert, one of the black pines was lit up by people pedalling bicycles to make the power. The garden is ticketed and about fifteen minutes on foot from Cambridge station.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise them as the two black pines facing each other across the Main Walk, one with slender limbs sloping downward, the other with huge branches spreading upward into an open crown.

story:
In 1886 a storm brought down one of the two Caucasian wingnuts planted beside the stream that feeds the Botanic Garden's Lake. The gardeners did not clear the ground. They let the suckers come up, and what stands there now is an immense thicket of stems, the tallest of them as tall as the original tree.

That is why this entry is a stand rather than a single trunk. The suckers have been left to grow for well over a century, straddling the stream so that it is hard to say where one tree ends and the next begins. The garden counts it among its most outstanding features. The Tree Register measured the tallest stem at 27 metres in 2004, a figure quoted by Trees and Shrubs Online.

The record of the 1886 loss comes from a 1915 survey by the garden's curator. Nobody has published when the original pair went in. The garden was established in 1846 and the trees were standing before the storm, so they were planted somewhere in those forty years, which makes the stand at least 140 years old in its roots. The clone itself is the living continuation of those first two trees.

In late summer long green chains of winged nutlets hang from the branches. The garden is ticketed, fifteen minutes on foot from the station.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as a thicket of tall wingnut stems rather than a single trunk, straddling the stream that runs into the Lake.

best_time.label: late summer, when long green chains of winged nutlets hang from the branches

story:
The Botanic Garden calls this the first dawn redwood to grow on British soil since the Mesozoic era, the age of the dinosaurs. Its seed was collected in China in 1946 and 1947 and sent by a Dr Silow to Professor F. T. Brooks in Cambridge. Two seedlings were planted out beside the Lake in 1949, according to that year's annual report.

The garden has kept a record of its growth ever since. It was 1.5 metres tall in 1952, 17 metres by 1977 and close to 23 metres in 2002, the last figure published. In that same year it was chosen as one of fifty Great British Trees to mark the Queen's Golden Jubilee.

That puts it at about 77 years old, young by the standards of this site but with a lineage most old trees cannot match. Emmanuel and Clare colleges also hold dawn redwoods from the same collection, by their own accounts, so the claim to be first is the garden's.

The tree stands on the south-western shore of the Lake, next to the garden's giant redwood, two very different trees with the same family name side by side. Unlike most conifers it drops its needles in winter. In late autumn they turn a foxy reddish brown before they fall. The garden is ticketed, fifteen minutes on foot from Cambridge station.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it in autumn by the needles turning reddish brown, and in winter by its bare branches, unlike the evergreen giant redwood. It stands beside that redwood on the south-western shore of the Lake.

best_time.label: late October into November, when the needles turn foxy reddish brown and fall

story:
In 1915 the garden's curator, Richard Lynch, recorded this pine at 5.4 metres. It has since reached 14.4, and the Botanic Garden says no other specimen in the British Isles appears to have grown so well. In the language of tree recorders, that makes it a champion, the best example of its kind in the country.

This is a rarity entry rather than an ancient one. The Chilgoza pine, also called Gerard's pine, is not a tree most visitors will have met, and what earns this one its place is how well it has done in a Cambridge garden, nearly tripling its height since the First World War.

That 1915 measurement is the oldest fact on record about it, and it tells you the tree was already established then. When it was planted, the garden does not say, and no one has published an estimate of its age. If you know, tell us.

The champion status rests on the garden's own account rather than a published register entry, so read the crown as the garden's claim. It stands on the Main Walk, the same avenue as the paired black pines Henslow planted, and the garden is ticketed, about fifteen minutes on foot from Cambridge station.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the Chilgoza pine on the Main Walk, 14.4 metres tall, the garden's champion of its kind. Look for the species label, since the pin marks the garden rather than the tree.
